scenes.title: Git: Remotes, Push/Pull & GitHub
scenes.narration: Remotes connect your local repository to a shared copy on a service like GitHub, so a whole team can collaborate on the same code.

scenes.title: Key Ideas
bullets: A remote is a hosted copy of your repository that everyone can reach.
Push uploads your local commits so teammates can see them.
Pull downloads their commits so your copy stays up to date.
scenes.narration: A remote is simply another copy of your repository living on a server that the team shares. When you push, you send your local commits up to that shared copy. When you pull, you bring everyone else's new commits down into your own, keeping your work synchronized.

scenes.title: The Collaboration Loop
scenes.narration: A healthy day starts by pulling the latest changes so you build on current code. You then make and commit your work locally. Pushing shares it back to the remote, where teammates pull it into their own repositories, and the loop continues.

scenes.title: Working with a Remote
scenes.code:
git clone https://github.com/team/pipeline.git
git remote -v            # list remotes
git pull origin main     # get latest
git push origin main     # share your work
scenes.narration: The clone command downloads an entire remote repository, including its full history, and wires up the connection automatically. Running remote -v shows which remotes you are linked to, with origin being the conventional default name. From there, pull and push move commits down from and up to the main branch on that remote.

scenes.text: Always pull before you push — syncing first prevents rejected pushes and keeps your history in step with the team.
scenes.narration: Make pulling before pushing a reflex. Syncing first avoids the frustration of a rejected push and keeps your local history aligned with everyone else's.
